header:
Date: 2025-03-05
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Dana Liu (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (BrightCart CTO), Jordan Price (BrightCart Lead ML Eng), Ravi Singh (BrightCart PM), Priya Nair (BrightCart Dev)
summary: Redwood AE + SE ran a hosted API demo focusing on chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, key generation parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry/backoff patterns and idempotency, and Console/Optimize surface for cost/perf tuning. BrightCart is evaluating a hosted integration first; security (SOC 2, data retention) and latency/cost tradeoffs are primary concerns. Agreed next steps include sharing pricing and security docs and scheduling a POC kick-off to benchmark latency/cost on a sample workload.
topics: Generation params: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences
Retries and idempotency (request IDs, exponential backoff)
Console demo: request logs, tokens/cost breakdown
Optimize suggestions: batching, caching, quantization recommendations
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, I'll do a quick intro and then Samir will jump into the console and the hosted API demo.
[00:12] Maya Lopez: Thanks Alex. Excited to see the hosted flow, we want something quick to integrate but predictable on cost.
[00:22] Alex Carter: Totally, that's what most teams start with. Today we'll show streaming, basic chat/text params, retries, and then show the console and Optimize suggestions.
[00:35] Samir Patel: Cool, jumping in. Quick note on nomenclature - we call it Redwood API (hosted), you'll see the same endpoints in Dedicated/Private but different routing and auth.
[00:47] Jordan Price: Quick question — do you support SSE and websockets for streaming or only long-polling?
[00:53] Samir Patel: We support SSE streaming for HTTP, and SDKs in Python/Node that wrap that, websocket is also an option in some SDKs. Streaming gives you token-level partials, lower TTFB.
[01:05] Ravi Singh: And how do you handle retries? We need idempotent behavior for some of our calls.
[01:11] Dana Liu: Good call. For hosted API we recommend attaching a client-generated request_id; server will dedupe within a short window. Retry pattern is typical exponential backoff, and we provide guidance in the SDKs. Also we expose a request status / request_id in logs so you can trace.
[01:30] Maya Lopez: Can you show the console where logs and token breakdowns live?
[01:35] Samir Patel: Yep, pulling up the console. Here is a past request - you can see token counts, model variant, latency in ms, and a cost estimate per request. We surface token-level cost with a breakdown between prompt and completion.
[02:05] Alex Carter: A lot of customers ask how to tune for quality vs cost: temperature, top_p, and max_tokens are the levers. Lower temperature for deterministic outputs, top_p affects diversity, and max_tokens caps completion length.
[02:25] Jordan Price: Does the console suggest parameter presets? We have prompt templates.
[02:30] Samir Patel: Redwood Optimize will analyze your traffic (sample prompts) and suggest batching, cache TTLs for prefix caching, and model/quantization recommendations. We can show a quick optimize demo later in POC.
[02:44] Priya Nair: About batching — if we batch multiple short chats, doesn't latency increase?
[02:50] Dana Liu: There's a tradeoff. Continuous batching groups requests to improve throughput and lower per-token cost; we configure max latency SLOs so tail latency is controlled. We can tune based on your SLOs.
[03:06] Maya Lopez: Security — we need SOC 2, SAML SSO, and audit logs, plus data retention controls.
[03:13] Samir Patel: We have SOC 2, SAML/SSO integrations, RBAC, and audit logs in the Console. For hosted, you can request short data retention or opt out; Dedicated/Private gives more control including VPC endpoints and customer-managed KMS.
[03:30] Alex Carter: For BrightCart's use case, many folks start hosted to iterate, then move to Dedicated for predictable throughput and private networking.
[03:40] Jordan Price: Latency targets — we aim for sub-200ms median for short completions. Can Redwood hit that on hosted?
[03:46] Samir Patel: It depends on model and region. For smaller open models we often see sub-100ms generation steps for 32-token outputs; bigger models are higher. We can run benchmarks with your sample prompts and give a quantified SLA expectation.
[04:05] Ravi Singh: Let's demo a streaming example.
[04:08] Samir Patel: Sure, here's an API call sequence — POST /v1/chat/complete with model param, messages, stream=true. The response is server-sent events streaming tokens. In the SDK it's one line: client.chat.stream(...). Note: transcripts sometimes call KV cache "K V cash" in past exports — ignore that, it's just transcription artifact.
[04:32] Alex Carter: We also expose retry headers and a request-id header so you can correlate logs.
[04:38] Jordan Price: Rate limiting? We expect spikes during flash sales.
[04:42] Dana Liu: Hosted has per-account rate limits but you can request bursts and quota increases; Dedicated has reserved GPU pools for sustained high throughput and auto-scaling config. We can propose a reserved capacity plan if you need guaranteed throughput.
[05:05] Priya Nair: How do we do deterministic test harnesses? We need to run regressions on prompt sets.
[05:11] Samir Patel: Use evals and the Console's quality monitoring; you can pin model versions and run A/B rollouts. We also store request/response artifacts for evals, subject to your retention policy.
[05:30] Maya Lopez: Can you change max_tokens mid-stream or with function calls?
[05:34] Samir Patel: For streaming, max_tokens is per call; function/tool calling is supported — you can return structured JSON in completions or use function calling primitives. For hosted API, we have structured output helpers.
[05:52] Jordan Price: Any SDK code examples?
[05:55] Samir Patel: The SDK has simple examples in Python and Node. Eg in Python: client.chat.create(..., stream=True, temperature=0.2) then iterate over events. We'll send the code snippets after the call.
[06:10] Ravi Singh: Error handling when a downstream kernel fails? How graceful are fallbacks?
[06:16] Dana Liu: We do automatic fallback routing to compatible model variants and regions based on your policy, and we surface metrics in Console so you can see fallbacks. Fallbacks can increase latency; we recommend canary rollouts for critical flows.
[06:34] Maya Lopez: About cost — do you charge per token or by request?
[06:38] Alex Carter: Hosted pricing is per-token for generation + per-embedding for embeddings. The Console shows a token cost breakdown; Optimize can suggest quantized/cheaper model variants for non-critical flows.
[06:52] Jordan Price: Is there support for stop sequences? We have a bunch of templates relying on stop tokens.
[06:56] Samir Patel: Yes, stop sequences are supported; also streaming will send a final event indicating completion, and you can pass multiple stop tokens.
[07:10] Priya Nair: Any known issues with punctuation in transcripts? Past Fireflies outputs sometimes mangle product names and acronyms.
[07:16] Alex Carter: Yeah, you'll see some transcription artifacts, nothing to worry about.
[07:22] Samir Patel: Back to demo — showing a live chat where we change temperature live. Notice that lower temperature makes responses more repetitive, higher temp more creative.
[07:40] [live screen demo noise and typing sounds]
[08:05] Jordan Price: For retries, is there a recommended HTTP status to trigger backoff that you set?
[08:10] Dana Liu: We return 429 for rate limit, 503 for transient infra errors; 400s for bad request. We recommend backoff on 429/503 and not on 4xx.
[08:26] Maya Lopez: Does Redwood provide sample backoff code?
[08:28] Samir Patel: Yes, included in SDKs and our integration guide.
[08:34] Ravi Singh: Can we set per-route quotas so our checkout flow has higher priority?
[08:38] Alex Carter: Yup, per-route routing and priority policies are supported in Console — you can pin routes to Dedicated or to a higher priority pool.
[08:50] Jordan Price: Any limitations on context window?
[08:53] Samir Patel: Model-dependent. We have model catalog with sequence length and performance profiles. Console shows the max_context for each model.
[09:05] Priya Nair: How about deterministic tokenization across SDKs — do all SDKs use the same tokenizer and token counts in Console?
[09:12] Dana Liu: Yes, tokenization is deterministic. We provide a token counter in Console so you can estimate tokens before sending.
[09:28] Maya Lopez: Let's talk POC. We want to run a week-long test against hosted with our sample storyboard.
[09:33] Alex Carter: Sounds good. Typical POC plan: 1) share sample prompts + traffic profile, 2) Redwood runs bench and config recommendations, 3) BrightCart runs integration and we monitor in Console, 4) iterate on optimizations.
[09:50] Jordan Price: Do you charge for POC?
[09:53] Alex Carter: Usually we use credits for initial POCs; for larger benchmarks we might discuss a short-term trial credit. We'll put details in the pricing doc.
[10:05] Ravi Singh: How do we measure per-token cost when using function calling or structured outputs?
[10:11] Samir Patel: We count tokens in prompt + completion; function call arguments are part of prompt/completion depending on flow. Console shows both pieces.
[10:24] [brief silence, screen switching]
[10:40] Samir Patel: Now showing optimize recommendations — for your chat intents, Optimize suggests batching at 50ms windows and enabling prefix caching for repeated templates. It also suggests a quantized 4-bit model variant for low-criticality flows to save costs.
[11:00] Maya Lopez: That sounds promising; what's the expected cost delta?
[11:04] Samir Patel: Typically 20-60% savings depending on traffic. We'll model it specifically in the POC.
[11:14] Jordan Price: Do you provide regression alerts? We need to know if quality drifts after a model update.
[11:18] Dana Liu: Yes, quality monitoring with prompt sets and eval baselines, can alert on metric drift.
[11:26] Maya Lopez: Security doc please.
[11:29] Alex Carter: We'll share SOC 2, encryption at rest/in transit, SSO details, and the Hosted vs Dedicated comparsion doc.
[11:38] [chuckle] Jordan Price: "Comparsion" — classic transcription artifact.
[11:42] Samir Patel: Wrapping up, recap of next steps: Alex will send pricing and trial details; Samir will send security pack and code snippets; BrightCart to share prompts + traffic profile.
[11:55] Maya Lopez: Great, we'll aim to share artifacts by Monday.
[12:00] Alex Carter: Awesome, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with a calendar invite for POC kick-off.
[12:06] [call ends]

Notes: Transcription contains small artifacts (product names, acronyms). The demo covered streaming via SSE, SDK usage for Python/Node, parameter tuning (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry semantics (request_id, 429/503 backoff), rate limiting vs Dedicated capacity, Console traces and token cost breakdowns, and Optimize recommendations for batching and quantization. Agreed POC + docs + pricing as next steps.
